claim.text: The Berlin Defence is Black's most solid answer to the Ruy Lopez. In this course White meets it with a calm protecting pawn move instead of the heavily analysed endgame lines.

You will learn the main line where White exchanges bishop for knight to give Black doubled pawns, the solid setups Black often chooses instead, and four common club mistakes with the exact way to punish each one.
Every line ends when the engine agrees the position is resolved: either one side is clearly better or the position is equal and both plans are clear.

nodes.title: 4.d3: the calm Anti-Berlin

claim.text: White simply protects the centre pawn with another pawn. There is no need to learn the long forcing lines after castling, and the pieces stay on the board for a manoeuvring game where plans matter more than memory.
In 1600–2200 club games it scores about 56% for White, as well as castling does.
In the main line White develops with Nbd2 and castles before starting any action.
It also takes away ...Nxe4: that move would now be answered by dxe4.
In 1600–2200 club games this was chosen in about 24% of games from this position, scoring 56% for White.
Solid centre first, active pieces second: once the centre is safe White can choose between pressure on Black's pawn and a later central break.
